issues.passage: The analyst hoped to impute the missing figures by re-running the spreadsheet.
issues.why: In statistics and data analysis, to impute missing figures is standard correct usage (fill in missing values). An analyst + missing figures + spreadsheet strongly licenses that reading, so a careful student would accept this sentence as valid English.

fix.correctPassage: Historians hesitate to impute deliberate deceit when the surviving records are incomplete.
wrongPassages: The analyst hoped to impute the quarterly total by simply multiplying unit sales by list price.
She tried to impute the error so that no one on the team would be blamed.
Before the vote, the clerk will impute each ballot into the counting machine.

issues.passage: Skipping every practice session had a salutary effect on her race times.
issues.why: Salutary is used correctly here to mean beneficial: the sentence asserts that skipping practice improved (or otherwise benefited) her race times. The claim may be surprising, but the vocabulary usage is valid and natural.

fix.correctPassage: The audit’s findings had a salutary effect, prompting tighter controls on discretionary spending.
wrongPassages: Chronic sleep loss had a salutary effect, leaving her unable to finish a simple exam.
The mold outbreak proved salutary for the tenants, who developed persistent respiratory illness.
The leak left a salutary stain that spread through the ceiling overnight.

issues.passage: Critics called the budget cuts salutary only because the services they funded disappeared.
issues.why: Salutary is used in its correct sense (beneficial). Critics can coherently praise cuts as salutary precisely because they eliminated services those critics viewed as wasteful; the sentence is valid, natural English, not a clear misuse.
